answer:
The best chain is QB11-QB12-QB7, with QB12 in the middle. I read the current default calibration of the real garnet computer (calibration set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade, default CZ implementation slepian_crf). It has 28 CZ pairs, and each pair has an IRB fidelity. I checked every chain of 3 connected qubits. For QB11-QB12-QB7, the IRB CZ fidelity of QB11-QB12 is 0.998693 and the fidelity of QB12-QB7 is 0.998016. Their product is 0.996712, which is the highest of all the chains. The next best chain is QB12-QB11-QB16, with a product of 0.994689.

I then built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly those physical qubits. The circuit first puts QB12 into an equal superposition. Then it entangles QB12 with QB11 and with QB7. Each entangling step is a CZ on that pair with single-qubit rotations around it. No other qubit pairs are used. All 3 qubits are measured. Before submitting, I simulated the circuit myself. A perfect machine gives 000 half the time and 111 half the time, and never gives anything else.

I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots. Job 01a16040-da95-726f-9264-c9066e29c928 completed. The counts, with bits in the order QB11, QB12, QB7, are 000: 48, 011: 42, 100: 57, 111: 53. The mock does not simulate the circuit. It returns random bitstrings, so the outcomes 011 and 100 show up even though a real GHZ state would not produce them. The mock run shows that the circuit is valid for those qubits and that the job runs. It does not show entanglement. On the real garnet you would expect mostly 000 and 111, at a level close to the fidelity product.

The principle is that a GHZ state links all 3 qubits so their measurements always agree: all 0 or all 1. Each 2-qubit gate adds a small error, so picking the pairs with the best measured CZ fidelity gives the circuit the best chance of keeping that agreement on real hardware.
